# The Summer Water-Lily
*(A polished rendering of William Barnes' Dorset dialect poem)*

O summer clote! When the brook is gliding
So slow and smooth along its sedge-lined bed,
Upon thy broad leaves so safely riding
The water's surface with thy golden head,
By alder shade, O,
And bulrush glade, O,
There thou dost float, golden summer clote!

The grey-boughed willow leans down lowly
Above the water where thy leaves reside;
The bending bulrush, swaying slowly,
Doth line in summer thy river's side;
And perch in shoals, O,
Do fill the holes, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer clote!

Oh, when thy brook-fed flower is blowing,
The burning summer is settling in;
The time of verdure, the time of mowing,
When in the hay-field, with sun-browned skin,
The folk do drink, O,
Upon the brink, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer clote!

With arms outspread, and cheeks all glowing,
How proud was I when I first learned to swim
Across the deep place where thou wast growing,
With thy long root from the bottom dim;
While cattle, knee-high, O,
Stood in the brook nearby, O,
Where thou dost float, golden summer clote!

Of all the brooks through the meadows winding,
Of all the meadows by a river's brim,
There's none so fair, by my heart's own finding,
As where the maidens watch thee swim,
And pause to take, O,
With long-stemmed rake, O,
Thy blossom afloat, golden summer clote!

---

**Note:** I've preserved the original poem's structure, rhyme scheme, refrain pattern, and all imagery while translating Barnes' Dorset dialect (e.g., "zummer" → "summer," "vu'st" → "first," "athirt" → "across") into standard literary English for broader accessibility and a more polished, professional register. Let me know if you'd like me to retain more of the original dialect flavor, or adjust the tone further in either direction.

**A Modern Paraphrase of "The Zummer Clote" (The Summer Water-Lily)**

Oh, golden water-lily of summer! As the stream flows gently and evenly along its reed-lined channel, you ride safely upon its surface, your yellow blossom crowning the water. Near the shadowed alders and among the bulrush thickets, there you drift, glowing lily of the summer season.

The willow, silver-branched, bends low, its foliage nearly concealing yours from view. The swaying bulrushes trace a slow path along the river's edge throughout the warm months, while perch gather in schools, crowding every hollow where your blossoms rest.

When your thirsty flower opens above the stream, it signals that scorching summer has truly arrived—the season of lush growth and haymaking, when workers with sun-darkened skin pause at the water's edge to drink, right where you float, brilliant golden bloom.

With arms stretched wide and cheeks puffed out with effort, how proud I felt the first time I managed to swim across that deep stretch where you grow, your long stem reaching down into the murky depths below—while cattle stood knee-deep nearby in the same waters where you drift.

Among all the streams that wind through the pastures, among all the fields bordering a riverbank, none holds greater beauty in my heart's memory than the spot where young women wade in to gather you, reaching out with long-handled rakes to claim your floating blossom, golden flower of summer.

# The Golden Clote

Upon the brook's unhurried current, where the waters move with dreamlike languor, the golden "zummer clote" rests in quiet splendor. Its broad, generous leaves cradle the bloom like a raft upon the surface, floating near the cool shadows cast by alders and the dense growth of bulrush beds that line the banks. Here, in this sheltered nook, the flower has found its perfect home, undisturbed by the world beyond.

The landscape that frames this golden bloom speaks of pastoral harmony. Willows lean wearily toward the water's edge, as if bowing in perpetual greeting to the stream below. Bulrushes sway with each passing breeze, their rhythmic dance a constant companion to the brook's murmur. Beneath the surface, in the deeper holes where the clote takes root and drifts, perch fish move in silvery schools, filling these watery hollows with quiet life.

It is in the fullness of summer that the clote reaches its golden peak—a season that coincides, fittingly, with the labor of haymaking. When the sun bears down mercilessly upon the fields, weary and sunburnt workers make their way to the brook's edge, seeking respite. They pause here to drink from the cool waters, perhaps glancing at the golden bloom floating nearby, a small mercy of beauty amid their toil.

For the speaker, this place holds the weight of cherished memory. As a child, there was fierce pride in first learning to swim across the deep water where the clote grows thick and golden—a rite of passage marked by the flower's watchful presence. In those same waters, cows would wade knee-deep, grazing contentedly at the water's edge, unbothered by the children's splashing games nearby.

Yet of all the meadows and brooks that grace this countryside, one place remains dearest to the speaker's heart: the spot where young maidens gather at the water's edge, wading in with long-stemmed rakes to harvest the clote's golden blooms. It is this image—of laughter, labor, and beauty intertwined—that lingers most powerfully in memory, a scene that captures the simple, timeless poetry of rural life along the brook.

# The Zummer Clote: A Celebration of Rural Dorset Life

William Barnes's dialect poem "The Zummer Clote" stands as a luminous example of nineteenth-century pastoral verse, one that transforms a simple wildflower into a vessel for an entire world of countryside memory and feeling. The "zummer clote"—the yellow water lily that drifts upon the surface of a slow-moving brook—becomes the poem's central emblem, its golden blossoms serving as both literal description and symbolic anchor for a meditation on rural belonging.

Written in the rich Dorset dialect that Barnes so lovingly cultivated throughout his poetic career, the poem unfolds through a sequence of carefully observed pastoral images. The brook itself is framed by alders, their leaves whispering above the water, while bulrushes stand sentinel along the banks, adding texture and verticality to the horizontal drift of the current. Beneath the surface, perch move through the shadowed pools, their presence suggesting the hidden vitality of the stream even as the eye is drawn to the floating lily above. This layering of imagery—sky, flower, water, fish—creates a sense of complete ecological harmony, a world where every element has its proper place and season.

The poem does not confine itself to the brook alone but widens its gaze to encompass the broader rhythms of agricultural life. Hay-making appears as a marker of the summer season, evoking the sweat and labor of rural work alongside its sensory pleasures: the scent of cut grass, the warmth of long days, the communal effort that bound village life together. This is counterbalanced by the lighter, more carefree image of children swimming in the brook, their laughter and splashing offering a vision of youthful freedom that stands in gentle contrast to the adult world of toil. Together, work and play, labor and leisure, are woven into a single seamless picture of summer in the countryside.

What gives the poem its particular emotional resonance is Barnes's use of dialect itself. By rendering these scenes in the authentic speech of rural Dorset, Barnes does more than add local color—he asserts the dignity and expressive richness of a language often dismissed as merely provincial. The dialect becomes inseparable from the landscape it describes, suggesting that the words themselves grew from the same soil as the alders and bulrushes, the same water as the drifting clote. This linguistic choice deepens the poem's nostalgic quality, for the dialect carries with it echoes of childhood, of a vanishing way of speaking and living that Barnes was determined to preserve in verse.

The poem's emotional culmination arrives in its final image: maidens gathering the golden blooms with long-stemmed rakes. This tender scene brings together several of the poem's central concerns in a single tableau. The young women, engaged in what might seem a humble rural task, become figures of grace and purpose, their reaching gestures echoing the reaching stems of the rakes themselves. The golden clote, plucked from the water, transforms from a passive natural object into something actively desired and gathered—perhaps for decoration, perhaps simply for the pleasure of possessing such beauty. There is an unmistakable tenderness in this closing image, a sense of continuity between the natural world and human affection, between the flower's quiet drifting and the deliberate care of those who gather it.

Ultimately, "The Zummer Clote" achieves its significance not through dramatic incident but through the accumulated weight of sensory detail and emotional suggestion. Barnes constructs a world so vividly rendered—in sight, sound, and even implied scent and touch—that the reader experiences the brook and its surroundings as a living memory rather than a mere description. The poem stands as a testament to a particular vision of rural England: unhurried, abundant, and deeply connected to the passage of the seasons. In celebrating so small a thing as a floating yellow lily, Barnes manages to capture something much larger—the irrecoverable sweetness of a remembered childhood summer, forever golden in the amber light of poetic recollection.
outputs.L5:
# Upon Reflection

Upon a hillside worn by centuries of rain, I found myself contemplating the strange persistence of old words—words like "thou" that once flowed as naturally from human lips as breath itself, now relegated to poetry, prayer, and Shakespeare's plays.

There is something melancholic in watching a word die. "Thou" was not merely a formal cousin to "you"—it carried intimacy, tenderness, the closeness reserved for God, family, and lovers. When English speakers stopped saying "thou," they lost more than a pronoun; they lost a distinction, a way of marking the sacred and the familiar apart from the common and the distant.

The evolution of language rarely announces itself. No single generation decided, "Thou shalt be spoken no more." Instead, the word simply faded—used less at the dinner table, less between friends, until it survived only in hymns and history books, a fossil embedded in the sedimentary layers of English speech.

Upon this hillside, watching the sun retreat behind clouds heavy with the coming evening, I thought about how language itself is a river, constantly reshaping its banks. The words we use today—casual, efficient, stripped of ceremony—will one day seem as antiquated as "thou" seems now. Perhaps future generations will marvel at our own vanished expressions, wondering why we spoke as we did, unaware that they too are drifting toward some future archaism.

The past speaks to us still, if we listen. Thou art gone, old word, but not forgotten—preserved in verse, in scripture, in the echo of voices that once called out across centuries, reaching toward something greater than themselves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in William Barnes' Dorset dialect style celebrating the yellow water lily ("zummer clote") floating in a river.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Zummer Clote

*(in the style of William Barnes)*

O zummer clote, wi' yollow crown,
A-floatin' where the brook do run,
Thy leaves do lie so green an' round,
Bezide the mowin'-grass i' zun.

Thy head do nod above the tide,
An' drink the light o' zummer skies,
While minnows in the shallers glide
An' zwallows skim wi' zwiftly flies.

The maidens by the water's brim
Do stoop to pull thy stalk zo long,
An' zing a low, glad zummer hymn,
Their laughter blendin' wi' the zong.

Thy root do bide down under ground,
'Ithin the mud so cool an' deep,
While up above thy vlower is vound
A-restin' where the ripples creep.

No garden vlower o' proud degree
Can match thy plainness, growed so free,
Vor thou dost bloom by bank an' tree,
A crown upon our Dorset lea.

So let the little brook run on,
By water-meads an' churchyard wall,
Wi' zummer clote to grace along
Its banks — the freest vlower of all.

---

*A few notes on the dialect choices: "z" replaces soft "s" (zummer, zong), "v" replaces "f" (vlower, vor), final "-ing" softens to "-in'" (floatin', growed), and "wi'" and "'ithin" stand for "with" and "within" — all hallmarks of Barnes' way of rendering the Dorset tongue on the page.*

counterfactuals.output:
**By Willowmere Brook**

'Tis summer now, and warm the sun doth lay
Upon the fields where new-mown hay doth dry,
And all along the brook, the bairns at play
Do splash and shout beneath a cloudless sky.

O, I do mind me of them golden days
When I meself were young and free as they,
When time were but a thing we ne'er did praise,
Nor reckoned much, from morn till fall o' day.

The hay-carls sweat beneath the noontide glare,
Their scythes a-swishin' through the fragrant grass,
While larks do wheel and warble in the air,
And clouds like woolly lambs do slowly pass.

Down by the brook where alders lean and sway,
The children strip and plunge into the stream,
Their laughter carries on the breath o' day,
As bright as any poet's fondest dream.

The waters, cool and clear as mountain glass,
Do tumble o'er the stones with merry song,
Whilst dragonflies do dart above the grass,
And summer days do seem to last so long.

Old Goodman Thatcher, bent with many a year,
Doth lean upon his rake and watch them play,
A wistful smile, a half-forgotten tear,
For he remembers such another day.

The haycocks rise like little hills o' gold,
Piled high by hands both weathered, worn, and true,
And in their shade the weary folk do hold
Their noontide rest, as country-folk still do.

Then home they trudge when evening shadows fall,
Their bellies full of bread and cheese and ale,
The church bell tolling faint and soft withal,
As mist doth rise along the darkling vale.

O brook, still run thy course through field and glen,
Still sing thy song as thou hast sung of yore,
Though I be old, and young no more, and when
My time doth come, I'll seek thy banks once more.

For though the years do steal our youth away,
And turn our summer gold to winter grey,
The brook remembers every bygone day—
'Tis we alone who wander far astray.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Goolden Flow'r

Below the alders, dark an' green,
Where cool the brook do slidy by,
A goolden flow'r, wi' petals sheen,
Do float aneath the zummer sky.

It broke away vrom zome bank-zide,
Where bulrush stems do stand so tall,
An' now upon the driftin' tide
It runs to meet what waters call.

The haymakers, wi' zweat-bright brow,
Do pause to zee it slidy by,
An' lean upon the new-turned mow,
To watch the goolden flow'r go nigh.

"Look there," zays Tom to little Jan,
"How bright en float, how free en go—
Just like the days when we vust ran
As children, where the brook do flow."

The zun do zink behind the hill,
The haymakers turn hwome at last,
But still the flow'r do float on, till
The dusk do come, an' day is past.

An' I do think, as I stand by,
Ov all the years so quickly gone—
Like that gay flow'r beneath the sky,
We drift, we float, we wander on.

---

*A note on the dialect:* I drew on Barnes' Dorset conventions — "zummer" for summer, "vrom" for from, "wi'" for with, "hwome" for home, and dropped or softened consonants throughout, echoing his gentle, musical rendering of rural West Country speech. Like much of his verse, this poem leans on the small, unhurried rhythms of farm life — haymaking, dusk, a stream's quiet passage — to hold a larger meditation on time within a simple, homely image.

counterfactuals.output:
**Meadowsweet by Parrett Water**

Oh flower as grows where Parrett do flow,
Wi' thy creamy head a-noddin' low,
Thee smells like honey pon the breeze,
And sets my wold heart proper at ease.

'Twas by thy banks I zported as a bwoy,
Barefoot in the mud, wild wi' joy,
My mother's linen laid to dry
Wi' thy sweet scent, so 'twould not lie
In musty chest through winter's cold—
Meadowsweet, they called 'ee, since of old.

Come hay-makin' time, when zun rode high,
And drashers zung beneath blue sky,
We'd stop at noon 'neath yonder tree
And pick a sprig, my dad and me,
To tuck bezide the cider jar,
And bless the work, though hard it are.

The vields did ring wi' scythe and song,
The gurt cart wheels did creak along,
But thee wast there at river's edge,
A-noddin' soft in every hedge,
As if to zay, "Rest thee awhile,
The zummer's long, so bide and smile."

Now I be wold, my back be bent,
The years be gone, the labor spent,
But still I walk down Parrett way
To vind thee bloomin' bright as day.
And in thy scent my childhood stirs—
The hay, the toil, the days as were.

Zo bide thee there, sweet flower of old,
Long as the water do be told
To wander down from hill to sea—
Thee bringst my zummers back to me.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a multi-stanza poem imitating 19th-century rural dialect verse, focusing on a "zummer clote" (yellow water lily) as a symbol of idyllic countryside life, using dialect spellings like "zunburnt" and "eärms."
counterfactuals.output:
**Da Zummer Clote**

Down where the stream do slidy on
By meäds all green wi' zummer dew,
The gooldèn clote do catch the zun
An' float upon the water blue.
Wi' leaves as broad as any hand
It rocks upon the ripplin' tide,
An' seems to smile athirt the land
As if 'twer glad o' zummertide.

An' when the haymakers do come
Wi' zunburnt eärms an' rakes in hand,
They'll pass along the river's rim
An' watch the clote so gaily stand.
The maidens too, wi' cheeks like rose,
Do stoop to pick a bloom or two,
An' pin 'em where the ribbon goes,
Bezide their necks o' milky hue.

Oh, clote, thee bidest all the day
A-noddin' in tha sunny light,
While children at their happy play
Do fling their laughter left an' right.
No care hast thee for time nor tide,
But bloomest on wi' quiet grace,
As if the whole green worold's pride
Wer gathered up in thy small feäce.

An' when the evenèn shadows vall
Athert the meäd an' vlowin' stream,
The clote do vold her petals small
An' zink to zleep as in a dream.
Zo mid our lives, when work is done,
An' zunburnt eärms do rest at last,
Vind peace as sweet as any zun
That ever on the clote wer cast.

For simple things do hold the heart
Far more than gold or lofty fame—
A yellow flower, set apart
Upon the stream, wi'out a name
Save what we gie 'un, plain an' true:
"The zummer clote"—an' let it be
A token, whersoe'er we go,
O' whoam, an' vields, an' historee.
